extracted.intended_audience: students, contributors, and enthusiasts solving classical geometry, mechanics, and calculus exercises (readers of a 19th-century mathematical problem journal)
extracted.subtask_description: Providing worked solutions to classical geometry, mechanics, and calculus problems (clear diagrams, algebraic/trigonometric derivations, and numeric checks), often offering multiple independent methods and citing standard references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define diagram and variables explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Start each solution by defining points, centres, radii, angles, and any other variables used (e.g. 'Let AB be the beam, D its middle point', 'Let A be the origin of polar coordinates').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label the diagram and state what each symbol denotes before algebraic or geometric manipulation so that subsequent steps are unambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose pivot/point-of-moment to eliminate unknown reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: When solving statics/mechanics problems on contact surfaces, take moments about the point of contact (or other strategic point) so as to eliminate the normal pressure and friction from the equilibrium equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for a beam on a sphere, taking moments about the contact F removes unknown normal and friction forces, simplifying to W.(AD−DF) = P.(AD+DF) + w.DF; explicitly mention this motive when choosing the pivot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direction cosines relations for perpendicular planes/lines
rubrics_metrics.description: When three planes or lines are mutually perpendicular, use the direction-cosine relations (sum of squares equals 1 and pairwise dot-products zero) to relate their direction cosines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the relations explicitly (e.g. α'^2+β'^2+γ'^2 = 1 and αα'+ββ'+γγ' = 0) and use them to transform area/length expressions as needed (references: Gregory's Solid Geometry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Present multiple independent solutions (geometric, algebraic, calculus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer more than one method when possible (synthetic geometry, analytic/co-ordinate methods, calculus), labelling them 'First Solution', 'Second Solution', etc., and crediting independent contributors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide at least one constructive/geometric and one analytic or calculus-based approach when they illuminate different aspects of the problem; omit only near-duplicate solutions while acknowledging contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refer to standard sources for known results
rubrics_metrics.description: When invoking known theorems, formulas, or standard expressions, cite the standard text or reference (e.g. 'see Gregory's Solid Geometry', 'By Davies's Hutton').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit citation helps justify steps that rely on established results and directs readers to fuller treatments; use such references for identities, formulae for areas/sections, and classical properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check limiting and special cases to validate formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify derived expressions by checking simple/special cases or limits (e.g. set a parameter to zero and confirm the result reduces to the known simpler formula).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: when the beam weight w = 0 the general expression for the angle should reduce to the stated formula; include these checks explicitly as validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show algebraic/trigonometric manipulations explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Carry through intermediate algebraic and trig transformations (eliminations, substitutions, identitiy uses) so the derivation is traceable from assumptions to final formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write key intermediate equations and substitutions (e.g. elimination of cot, use of sin2θ identities) rather than skipping steps, especially in trig-heavy derivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use coordinate transforms and auxiliary constructions to simplify
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply coordinate changes (translating axes, using polar coordinates) or construct auxiliary figures/triangles to convert the problem into a simpler, standard form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: transform the parabola equation to new axes to simplify, or set A as origin of polar coordinates and measure from AX; state the transformation and its effect on the equation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive alternative/simplified working formulas for practical use
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, reduce expressions to compact 'working formulas' that are convenient for computation (e.g. neat expressions for reciprocals of n and N in spherical-trigonometry formulas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out when a derived form is especially suitable (e.g. 'especially if the reciprocals only of n and N be required') and present the simplified versions explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute numerical examples and report units
rubrics_metrics.description: When the problem involves real-world quantities, carry out numerical computation of final answers and state units (e.g. compute final velocity in feet per second and miles per hour, compute time in seconds and minutes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the numeric substitutions, intermediate numeric values (g, distances), and final unit-converted results to demonstrate applicability and correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclude proofs with an explicit final statement
rubrics_metrics.description: End each solution with a clear concluding sentence such as 'which proves the theorem' or an explicit statement of the result proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps the reader recognise the successful end of the derivation and ties the algebraic work back to the original enunciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit contributors and suppress repetitive redundancy
rubrics_metrics.description: When many similar solutions are received, credit the authors and omit near-duplicate solutions while noting their receipt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate when omitted solutions are similar in principle and list names as acknowledgement rather than reproducing redundant content.
